headline: The official same-point comparison with 2022 still points to a national vote near even while the polls say D+8.8: by registration, Florida's early vote is D+3.2 after three days of in-person voting, against D+1.4 at 13 days out in 2022, Colorado D+8.6 against D+3.4 and Iowa's absentee pool D+27.1 against D+22.0, which pool to an implied national vote of about D-0.2 (±1.5). Against 2024 the picture is better for Democrats: Nevada's corrected Oct 21 file reads D+2.8 against R+4.0, Colorado D+8.6 against D+3.0, pooling to about D+2.7 (±1.8), and Pennsylvania's mail ballots are D+43.5 against D+31.9. The news comparisons lean more Democratic: Jon Ralston's Nevada count has Democrats up about 4 points with urban Nevada 1.4 points ahead of 2022, North Carolina's early vote is 38% ahead of 2022 with registered Republicans below their 2022 count, Georgia's in-person vote is 12% ahead and Texas's Democratic-primary voters led day one where Republicans led in 2022, though mail is down and in-person voting up almost everywhere.

measures.label: Iowa: early voters by registration, D-minus-R margin (mail plus in person)
measures.src: Call the Map (Iowa Secretary of State daily absentee statistics), Oct 18
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official files; affiliation not stated. 33,418 ballots through Oct 15, mostly cast in person, vs. the same point in 2024 (D+10.4 at the same point in 2022)

measures.label: Pennsylvania: returned mail ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin (52 comparable counties)
measures.src: Call the Map (Pennsylvania Department of State mail-ballot file), Oct 16
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 52 of 67 counties (92% of ballots); the app's own comparison takes over once the 2024 baseline reaches this point

measures.label: Maine: absentee ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin
measures.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 18
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 96,849 ballots through Oct 15 vs. the same point in 2024 (Oct 17, 2024); 2022 at the same working day was D+33.6

measures.label: Florida: early voters by registration, D-minus-R margin (mail plus in person)
measures.src: Call the Map (Florida Division of Elections file), Oct 20
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 1,384,887 ballots through Oct 19 (mail 1,025,383, in person 359,504) vs. the same point in 2024, when in-person voting had also just begun; the count is 38% below 2024's. The app's own file reads D+4.3 on the same day

measures.label: Virginia: Democratic share of early voters, two-party (L2 modeled party)
measures.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Virginia has no party registration, so party is modeled in both years

measures.label: Ohio: early voters by party (last primary ballot), D-minus-R margin
measures.src: News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13 (Ohio Secretary of State data)

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024, as read from the official files by Call the Map (an independent tracker; Iowa 33,418 ballots through Oct 15, Pennsylvania's 52 comparable counties through Oct 16, Maine 96,849 through Oct 15, Florida's 1,384,887 mail and in-person ballots through Oct 19 against R+4.9 at the same point in 2024). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Florida's, Nevada's, Colorado's, Iowa's, Pennsylvania's and North Carolina's official comparisons with 2022 and 2024 are computed from the state files above and now run a day later than these. Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, Florida included because 2024's Republicans had moved to the mail; against 2022 the picture is mixed and much narrower.

bullets.title: The official comparison with 2022 still implies a national vote near even; against 2024 it reads about D+2.7.
bullets.html: By registration, Florida's Oct 21 file counts 1,677,855 ballots at D+3.2 (mail 482,104 Democrats to 404,899 Republicans; in person 210,738 to 234,905), against D+1.4 at 13 days out in 2022, when in-person voting had not begun; Colorado's 657,781 returned ballots are D+8.6 against D+3.4 on the same day in 2022; Iowa's 28,568 mailed-back absentees are D+27.1 against D+22.0. The app's calibrated slopes turn those into +1.5, +4.4 and +1.1 points of margin and a pooled implied national vote of about D-0.2 (±1.5), against polls at D+8.8 and the app's forecast at D+6.8. Against 2024 the same files read better for Democrats: Nevada's corrected Oct 21 file (235,191 ballots, 33.5% Democrats to 30.7% Republicans, D+2.8) against R+4.0, worth about +5.8, Colorado D+8.6 against D+3.0 (+4.7), pooling to about D+2.7 (±1.8); Pennsylvania's 678,557 mail ballots at D+43.5 against D+31.9 are worth about +2.6 (±3.3), and its 2022 match comes at 12 days out. Arizona's county compilation reads D+0.8 on 649,159 ballots with no same-point baseline.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 21
UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 21)
bullets.aff: Official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Nevada: Democrats lead by about 4 points after five days, all of it from the mail.
bullets.html: Jon Ralston's count on the evening of Oct 21 had Democrats ahead by 10,168 ballots, about 4 percent, of 244,767 cast, just under 12% of active voters; urban Nevada's Democratic lead is just under 10 points, 1.4 points ahead of 2022, when Lombardo won by 1.5 after an 8.6-point urban lead at this stage. That morning: Clark D+11, Washoe D+7, the rurals R+31; about 123,000 mail ballots (63%) at D+9 and 72,000 in-person ballots at R+3, and the day's mail ran D+25.5. Republicans won Washoe's in-person vote by 11 on Oct 21 but their Clark in-person margins were 'much smaller' than in the past. Ralston: Republicans 'are going to need a big Election Day to head off a blue wave,' but 'there is still three-quarters of the vote to come so no wavy conclusions yet.' The state's corrected Oct 21 file reads D+2.8 against R+4.0 at this point in 2024.
sources: UF Election Lab daily file (Nevada, Oct 21)
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; county and Secretary of State data

bullets.title: North Carolina's early vote is 38% ahead of 2022, and registered Republicans are below their 2022 count.
bullets.html: Michael Bitzer's Day 6 tally: 924,160 ballots vs. 668,913 at the same point in 2022, 38% ahead; in-person voting 876,977 vs. 599,808 (up 46%) and accepted mail 47,183 vs. 69,105 (down 32%). In-person voters are 44% Democrats, 34% unaffiliated and 22% Republicans, against 39%, 29% and 32% on the same day in 2022; Democrats are 151,000 ballots ahead of their 2022 same-day total, unaffiliated voters 126,000, Republicans 1,383 behind. Black, Millennial and Gen Z shares of the in-person vote run ahead of 2022, while the mail pool is whiter and older. WFAE: 14.05% of Democrats, almost 8% of unaffiliated voters and 6.5% of Republicans had voted through Oct 19; UNC Charlotte's Eric Heberlig expects Republicans to outvote Democrats on Election Day. Bitzer calls his projection 'a working model, not a validated prediction.' The app's own file (1,101,318 accepted ballots through Oct 21) carries the official comparison.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan academic and public radio; official data

bullets.title: Georgia passed 1.3 million ballots; in-person voting ran 12% ahead of 2022 at the state's last release.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State counted 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, plus 48,916 accepted absentee ballots. GeorgiaVotes.com's tally as of 7:15 a.m. Oct 22: 1,330,455 ballots, 1,267,737 in person and 62,718 by mail, which it puts 5% above 2022's same-point total of 1,268,916; Black voters 33.8%, white 53.0%; women 55.3%; voters 65 and over 46.5%; 214,717 (16.1%) did not vote in 2022. The AJC finds about 400,000 early voters from strongly Harris areas vs. 380,000 from strongly Trump ones (return rates 21% vs. 16%), rural South and Middle Georgia lagging and Republican Cherokee and Forsyth up on 2022; about 95% of early voters also voted in 2024. Georgia has no party registration.
bullets.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker; AJC is nonpartisan

bullets.title: Texas: Democratic-primary voters led day one where Republicans led in 2022.
bullets.html: 812,998 Texans voted on the first two days. Republican data consultant Derek Ryan's day-one report found voters with only Democratic primary history ahead of Republican-primary-only voters by 69,046 ballots, where Republican-primary voters led by 81,429 on day one in 2022; 3% had never voted and 16% vote only in generals. Dallas County cast 76,079 first-day ballots vs. 32,605 in 2022, Collin 34,500 vs. 18,991, Denton 34,700 vs. 17,416, Travis 4.3% of registered voters vs. 2.8%. Ryan says Democrats are 'enthusiastic' but wants three or four more days of data, and that Republicans need at least 25% of turnout from outside the 25 largest counties; the Texas Politics Project finds 63% of Democrats and 48% of Republicans planning to vote early. Texas has no party registration.
bullets.aff: Derek Ryan is a Republican consultant; county data via nonpartisan outlets

bullets.title: Florida: Democrats bank the mail, Republicans pull ahead in person.
bullets.html: The Division of Elections' Oct 21 file had 1,125,903 mail ballots returned, 482,104 from Democrats and 404,899 from Republicans (D+77,205), and 551,952 in-person ballots, 234,905 Republican to 210,738 Democratic (R+24,167, up from R+7,317 a day earlier); the combined gap narrowed from D+4.3 to D+3.2, against D+1.4 at this point in 2022. Every county must open sites by Oct 24. Democratic consultant Steve Schale notes the state deleted its mail-request list, so every voter had to reapply; press comparisons are to 2022's final mail totals (Democrats 1.19 million of 2.77 million), not the same point.
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; Schale is a Democratic consultant

bullets.title: Turnout without party: Wisconsin's first in-person day was 65% above 2022 as its mail runs 26% behind; Michigan mail level with 2022.
bullets.html: Wisconsin: 55,659 voters cast in-person absentee ballots on Oct 20, the first day, vs. 33,644 on the first day in 2022 (Elections Commission figures), with Milwaukee up 63%, Dane 60% and Kenosha 87%, while mail ballots received were down nearly 26% from the same point in 2022; Call the Map counts 313,000 ballots through Oct 21, 11% below 2022. Michigan's latest release (7 a.m. Oct 20) had 789,572 ballots back (10.7% of active voters) vs. 771,967 at the same time in 2022, up 2.2%, with 2,121,458 requests, 17% ahead; statewide in-person voting opens Oct 24. Virginia had more than 568,000 early votes with 21 days to go vs. just over 307,000 in 2022 (VPAP), and Minnesota 202,252 accepted ballots through Oct 15 vs. 172,520. Pennsylvania's approved mail ballots, about 1.2 million as of Oct 19, are fewer than at the same point in 2022 or 2024.
sources: CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State release), Oct 20

bullets.title: The Democratic edge is partly a change in how people vote, and Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: Mail is down and in-person voting up almost everywhere: North Carolina's mail ballots are 32% below 2022 while in-person is up 46%; Wisconsin's mail is down 26% and its first in-person day up 65%; Pennsylvania's Democrats have requested 14% fewer mail ballots than in 2022 and returned 47% of them against 51% then, which Democratic strategist J.J. Abbott attributes to voters switching to in-person voting and Charles Stewart (MIT) says the data cannot explain. In Nevada, Ralston notes 2022's in-person voters switching to mail, and that Republicans won Election Day 2022 by 2-to-1; in Texas, 63% of Democrats but 48% of Republicans plan to vote early (Texas Politics Project), and 40% of Republicans plan to vote on Election Day. UNC Charlotte's Eric Heberlig expects North Carolina Republicans to outvote Democrats on Election Day, and an RNC spokeswoman says Republicans are cutting into Democrats' mail lead in Georgia.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan sources; Abbott is a Democratic strategist; GOP-aligned claims reported as such

calendar_note: Every Florida county must open in-person early voting by Oct 24 (counties could open Oct 19); Michigan's statewide sites, New York's and New Jersey's open Oct 24 and Kentucky's Oct 29. Texas, Alaska, Colorado's service centers and South Carolina opened Oct 19 and Wisconsin's in-person absentee voting Oct 20; Nevada's in-person early voting opened Oct 17, North Carolina's Oct 15 and Georgia's Oct 13. Georgia's and Texas's in-person periods end Oct 30, Maine's no-excuse absentee period Oct 29. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 46 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 16-22) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison with 2022 (Florida, Colorado, Iowa) implies a national vote of about D-0.2 (±1.5): Florida is D+3.2 by registration against D+1.4 at 13 days out in 2022, Colorado D+8.6 against D+3.4, Iowa's absentee pool D+27.1 against D+22.0; against 2024, Nevada's corrected file (D+2.8 vs. R+4.0) and Colorado pool to about D+2.7 (±1.8) and Pennsylvania's mail is D+43.5 against D+31.9, so the early vote fits a Democratic year without confirming polls at D+8.8. Republicans are winning Florida's in-person vote by about 24,000 ballots while Democrats bank the mail, Nevada's mail is two-thirds of the vote and D+9, North Carolina and Georgia run well ahead of 2022 and Wisconsin's first in-person day was 65% above 2022 even as its mail returns run 26% behind. The next tests are Pennsylvania's first 2022 match at 12 days out, Florida's first full week with every county open from Oct 24, Michigan's in-person start the same day and whether Nevada's urban lead holds through the weekend.

signals.title: Nevada Democrats lead by about 4 points after five days; urban Nevada is 1.4 points ahead of 2022
signals.value: Jon Ralston's count on the evening of Oct 21: Democrats ahead by 10,168 ballots, about 4 percent, of 244,767 cast (just under 12% of active voters, perhaps a quarter of the final vote). Urban Nevada's Democratic lead is just under 10 points, 1.4 points ahead of 2022, when Lombardo won by 1.5 after an 8.6-point urban lead at this stage. That morning the lead was 8,529 (4.4 points) of about 195,000: Clark D+11, Washoe D+7, the rurals R+31; about 123,000 mail ballots (63%) at D+9 and 72,000 in-person ballots at R+3. He writes that Republicans 'are going to need a big Election Day to head off a blue wave.'
signals.catch: Party is registration, not vote choice. Mail is just under two-thirds of the vote and accounts for the whole Democratic edge; Republicans won Washoe's in-person vote by 11 points on Oct 21 and have won the weekday in-person vote in every region. Ralston: 'three-quarters of the vote to come so no wavy conclusions yet'; Republicans won Election Day 2022 by 2-to-1 and almost 50,000 ballots. The state's own Oct 21 file reads D+2.8 (the app's official panel).
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet (Jon Ralston); county and Secretary of State data

signals.title: Georgia's early vote passed 1.3 million, 12% ahead of 2022 in person at the same point
signals.value: The Secretary of State counted 1,007,015 in-person early ballots before noon on Oct 20, up 12% from 894,412 at the same point in 2022, plus 48,916 accepted absentee ballots. GeorgiaVotes.com's file as of 7:15 a.m. Oct 22: 1,330,455 ballots (1,267,737 in person, 62,718 mail), 5% above its 2022 same-point figure of 1,268,916; Black voters 450,090 (33.8%), white 704,902 (53.0%); women 55.3%; voters 65 and over 46.5%, 18-29 7.0%; 214,717 (16.1%) did not vote in 2022.
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Mail is a far smaller share than in 2022, which flatters the in-person comparison; the tracker's all-ballot comparison (+5%) is much smaller than the state's in-person one (+12%) and its 2022 basis is not stated. The AJC reports turnout lagging in rural South and Middle Georgia and up in Republican Cherokee and Forsyth; about 95% of early voters also voted in 2024.
signals.src: Georgia Secretary of State, Oct 20; GeorgiaVotes.com, Oct 22; AJC, Oct 20
signals.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state file; AJC is a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic
signals.value: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes after one week: 194,841 vs. 50,368 in 2022. On Point Politics counts 764,330 ballots cast through Oct 21 (319,992 mail, 444,338 in person), without party.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests are 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots so far. No newer party breakdown has been published since Oct 15.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early vote is nearly 300,000 ballots ahead of 2022
signals.value: More than 678,000 Virginians had voted by Oct 18, nearly 300,000 more than at the same point in the 2022 midterm (VPAP data via WTVR). Danville has 2,800 vs. a little over 1,000 in 2022.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The count's exact as-of day is not stated. The modeled party lean is in the separate L2 signal.
signals.src: WTVR CBS 6 (Virginia Public Access Project data), Oct 18
signals.aff: Nonpartisan outlet; VPAP is a nonpartisan tracker of state data

signals.title: Maine's absentee vote is 37% ahead of 2022 and slightly more Democratic
signals.value: 126,998 ballots through Oct 19 (67,843 by mail, 68,223 in person): 66,690 Democrats (up 34% on 2022), 25,106 Republicans (up 24%), 35,202 unaffiliated (up 57%). That is a D+32.7 gap vs. D+32.0 at the same working day in 2022; the count is up 37%. Through Oct 15 the gap was D+34.2 vs. D+21.7 at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice. The edge over 2022 is less than a point and has narrowed as in-person absentee voting (half the ballots) grows. The 2022 match is by working day.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Minnesota's accepted ballots are running 17% ahead of 2022
signals.value: 202,252 absentee and mail ballots accepted through Oct 15 (80,870 in person, 121,382 by mail), vs. 172,520 at the same point in 2022. 519,813 ballots distributed vs. 474,935.
signals.catch: Minnesota has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. The lead over 2022 has narrowed from 29% (Oct 8). The source is a local news aggregator citing the Secretary of State's Oct 16 report; the report itself was not opened.
signals.src: Minneapolimedia News (Minnesota Secretary of State Oct 16 report), Oct 18
signals.aff: Official data via a local aggregator

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022, and Democrats' requests are down 14%
signals.value: 676,252 returned mail ballots through Oct 20 in the 66 comparable counties are D+43.6 by registration vs. D+53.7 at the same point in 2022, with the count level with 2022 (Call the Map, Oct 21). Votebeat/Spotlight PA: about 1.2 million approved mail ballots as of Oct 19, fewer than at the same point in 2022 or 2024; requests from Democrats are down 14% on 2022 and Republicans' up 11%; Democrats have returned 47% of theirs (51% in 2022, 55% in 2024), Republicans 43%, independents 36%. The app's official comparison with 2024 (D+43.5 vs. D+31.9 at 13 days out) runs the other way.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting after the party's own warnings about the mail (Charles Stewart: the data cannot show the cause). The official comparison takes over against 2022 at 12 days out. Older voters dominate the returns so far.
signals.src: Call the Map (Pennsylvania Department of State mail-ballot file), Oct 21; Votebeat/Spotlight PA, Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; Votebeat and Spotlight PA are nonpartisan newsrooms

signals.title: Wisconsin's absentee count trails 2022 by 11%: mail down 26%, first in-person day up 65%
signals.value: 55,659 voters cast in-person absentee ballots on Oct 20, the first day, vs. 33,644 on the first day in 2022 and 34,036 in 2025 (Wisconsin Elections Commission figures via WKOW); WPR puts the first day 65% above 2022, with Milwaukee up 63%, Dane 60% and Kenosha 87%, while mail ballots received as of Oct 20 are down nearly 26% from the same point in 2022 (Dane -26%, Milwaukee -22%). Call the Map counts 313,000 ballots through Oct 21, 11% below 2022.
signals.catch: No party registration. Mordecai Lee (UW-Milwaukee) attributes the mail decline to worries about the Postal Service and Trump's executive order, so much of it is a mode shift; both parties have pushed voters away from mail. The gap may close in person over the next two weeks.
signals.src: WKOW (Wisconsin Elections Commission data), Oct 21; WPR, Oct 21; Call the Map, Oct 21

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns are 2% ahead of 2022, requests 17% ahead
signals.value: 789,476 ballots returned by mail, drop box or at clerks' offices as of 7 a.m. Oct 20, plus 96 cast at early-voting sites, 789,572 in all (10.7% of active voters), vs. 771,967 at the same time in 2022, up 2.2%; 2,121,458 requests, 2,001,574 from the permanent list, 17% ahead of 2022 (Secretary of State release).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. Returns had been 30% ahead of 2022 on Oct 6 and have since converged; statewide in-person early voting opens Oct 24.
signals.src: CBS Detroit (Michigan Secretary of State release), Oct 20
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

signals.title: Texas: Democratic-primary voters led day one by 69,000 where Republicans led by 81,000 in 2022
signals.value: 812,998 Texans voted on the first two days. Derek Ryan's day-one report: voters with only Democratic primary history outnumbered those with only Republican primary history by 69,046 ballots; on day one in 2022 Republican-primary-only voters held an 81,429-vote advantage. First-time voters were 3% and general-election-only voters 16%. Ryan: 'The biggest storyline is that Democrats are enthusiastic,' with three or four more days of data needed. Dallas County cast 76,079 first-day ballots vs. 32,605 in 2022; Collin 34,500 vs. 18,991; Denton 34,700 vs. 17,416.
signals.catch: No party registration: primary history covers a minority of voters and the big counties also hold most Republican suburban voters. Ryan is a Republican consultant; he says Republicans need at least 25% of turnout from outside the 25 largest counties. The Texas Politics Project finds 63% of Democrats but 48% of Republicans planning to vote early, so day-one surges may fade.
signals.src: KXAN (Ryan Data & Research), Oct 21; KERA, Oct 20
signals.aff: Derek Ryan is a Republican data consultant; county figures via nonpartisan outlets

signals.title: Florida Republicans lead the in-person vote by 24,000 after three days while Democrats lead the mail by 77,000
signals.value: Division of Elections file for Oct 21: 551,952 in-person ballots, 234,905 Republican, 210,738 Democratic, 106,309 other or no party (R+24,167, up from R+7,317 the day before); 1,125,903 mail ballots returned, 482,104 Democratic, 404,899 Republican (D+77,205). The combined gap narrowed from D+4.3 on Oct 20 to D+3.2.
signals.catch: Only counties that chose to open early are voting; all must by Oct 24. Republicans won Florida's in-person vote by far more in 2022 and 2024, so an early lead of this size is not obviously good for them; no same-point in-person figure for 2022 was published. Registration is not vote choice. The overall same-point comparison is the app's official panel (D+3.2 vs. D+1.4 in 2022).
signals.src: Florida Division of Elections daily file via the app's official comparison, Oct 21

signals.title: Clark County's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: Clark County mail ballots through Oct 18: 46,590, Democrats 19,681 (up 3% on 2022), Republicans 13,459 (up 34%), others 13,450 (up 34%), a D+13.4 gap vs. D+23.2 at the same number of days before Election Day in 2022; the count is up 19%. Of 97,990 Clark ballots in the file, 62% were mail and 38% in person (Call the Map). Ralston has Clark's mail at 43-29.
signals.catch: Democrats are shifting from mail to in person, which Ralston's county-wide figures (Clark D by nearly 12 overall) absorb; this compares only the mail mode. Registration is not vote choice. Small numbers for a county of 1.4 million voters.
signals.src: Call the Map (Clark County mail file), Oct 20
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated
